{{Short description|Statistical estimation technique}}
In [[applied statistics]], '''Vincentization'''<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aos/1176348676 |title=Vincentization Revisited |last1=Genest |first1=Christian |publisher=The Annals of Statistics|volume=20 |number=2 |pages=1137–1142 |date=1992 |format=PDF|accessdate=5 Sep 2018}}</ref> was described by Ratcliff (1979),<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://star.psy.ohio-state.edu/wp/pdf/Papers/psychbull79.pdf |title=Group Reaction Time Distributions and an Analysis of Distribution Statistics |last1=Ratcliff |first1=Roger |journal=Psychological Bulletin|volume=86 |number=3 |pages=446–461 |date=1979 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.86.3.446 |pmid=451109 |accessdate=18 November 2016}}</ref> and is named after biologist S. B. Vincent (1912),<ref>{{cite journal |title=The function of the viborissae in the behavior of the white rat |last1=Vincent |last2=Burnham |first1=Stella |publisher=Behavior Monographs|volume=1 |date=1912}}</ref> who used something very similar to it for constructing [[learning curve]]s at the beginning of the 1900s. It basically consists of averaging <math>n\geq 2</math> subjects' estimated or elicited [[quantile function]]s in order to define group quantiles from which <math>F</math> can be constructed.

To cast it in its greatest generality, let <math>F_1,\dots, F_n </math> represent arbitrary (empirical or theoretical) [[Cumulative distribution function|distribution function]]s and define their corresponding quantile functions by

: <math> F_i^{-1}(\alpha) = \inf\{t\in \mathbb{R} : F_i(t)\ge\alpha) \},\quad 0<\alpha\leq 1. </math>

The Vincent average of the <math>F_i</math>'s is then computed as

: <math> F^{-1}(\alpha) = \sum w_i F_i^{-1}(\alpha),\quad 0<\alpha\leq 1,\quad i = 1,\ldots,n </math>

where the non-negative numbers <math>w_1,\dots,w_n</math> have a sum of <math>1</math>.
